messages.body_plain:
Hello again,
I think I was able to come up with a solution (albeit not a very elegant one). I fit a joint likelihood model where each year has a separate formula:
obs_y1 = intercept + spatial.field1 + spatial.field2
obs_y2 = intercept + beta_sf1y2 * spatial.field1 + beta_sf2y2 * spatial.field2
...
obs_yn = intercept + beta_sf2yn * spatial.field1 + beta_sf2yn * spatial.field2

where the effect in bold is specified as f(spatial.field1.n, copy = spatial.field1, hyper = list(beta = list(fixed = FALSE)))

To my understanding, this copies the effect of spatial.field1 (with a small error) and allows for estimation of the beta (which is what I had wanted).

This seems to run ok, although as you predicted the model is struggling to differentiate the two spatial processes. I am still figuring out how best to inform the priors but thought I'd share what I've done so far in case you have any thoughts.

Thank you for all the help!

Sincerely,
Louis

be a little skewed.

By default, the skewness of these marginals only come from integration over the
hyperparamters, as the approximation for fixed hyperpameters are Gaussian. THere
is a thesis discussing how to correct this, and work in on the way to make a
such approximation into R-INLA

sim_code_2 = nimbleCode({
 for(i in 1:N){
 lambda[i] <- exp(a0 + a1 * x[i] + phi[i])
 pi[i] <- ilogit(b0 + b1 * v[i] + gamma[i])
 z[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i] * pi[i])
gamma[i] ~ dnorm(0, sd = epsilon) }
 phi[1:N] ~ dcar_normal(adj = adj[1:l_adj], num = n_adj[1:N], tau = tau, zero_mean = 1)
 a0 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 10)

 b0 ~ dnorm(prior_mean, sd = prior_sd)
 b1 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 10)

 tau <- 1 / nu^2 epsilon ~ T(dnorm(0, sd = 1), 0,) })

func <- function(beta0, v1, beta1, theta) {

 # Formula
 formula_poiss_media <- z ~ intercept + alpha1 + spatial + func(b0, v1, b1, theta)

However, I am getting very different results for the coverage of b1.

I probably made a mistake in defining the causal effect.

Does anyone have any ideas and can help me?

Thanks

Hi,
not sure if this is the only difference between your Nimble model and
your INLA model, but you have prec.linear=0.1 in the INLA code but
sd=10 in the Nimble code, which corresponds to precision=0.01, not
0.1.
There might be more differences; I would expect the "besag"
parameterisation & priors to be difficult to be identical between the
two specifications, for example; it's unclear whether you've commented
out parts of your "spatial" model hyperparameter settings, and
scale.model also changes the interpretation of the parameters (but in
the INLA context, you likely are better off using it anyway).
Finn

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Standardized continuous covariates - do I need to reverse for outputs
messages.body_plain:
Yes, if you want to be able to interpret model parameters on the non-standardised scale, you have to do the corresponding transformation of the parameter estimates.

Likewise, if you don’t do that parameter postprocessing, then to do prediction for new covariate values, those need to be transformed using the same transformation as used to preprocess the covariate as well. For this reason, using black box standardisation methods such as “scale()” aren’t very useful, and manual transformation is more practical, as you can then store and use the standardisation information on new data.

Finn

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Standardized continuous covariates - do I need to reverse for outputs
messages.body_plain:
If the model you want is

  eta = beta_0 + beta_x * x

but you pre-standardise to x_std = (x-mean(x)) / sd(x), that means

  eta = beta_0 + beta_x * (x.std * sd(x) + mean(x)) = beta_0 + beta_x
* mean(x) + beta_x * sd(x) * x_std

This shows that the standardisation changes the interpretation of the
parameters _as seen by inla_, which is

eta = beta_0_std + beta_x_std * x_std

with beta_0_std = beta_0 + beta_x * mean(x) and beta_x_std = beta_x * sd(x).

So to recover beta_x, you need
  beta_x_std / sd(x),
and to recover beta_0, you need
  beta_0_std - beta_x * mean(x) = beta_0_std - beta_x_std / sd(x) * mean(x)

If all you want is prediction based on new data x_new, you can alternatively do

x_new_std = (x_new - mean(x))/sd(x)

and

beta_x_std * x_new_std

instead of converting beta_x_std to beta_x.

The trap you need to avoid is the temptation to use x_std = scale(x),
and then x_new_std = scale(x_new), which is completely different to
what I detailed above, as it would instead use mean(x_new) and
sd(x_new) in the conversion, which completely breaks the definition of
the model, which is based on standardising with the mean and sd of the
_original_ data.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: Composition data with zeros
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ruby,

Thank you for your question. In the CoDa context with many zeros, I believe you could consider the following approaches when using INLA:

Data Transformation:
You can apply a transformation such as DR_data from the DirichletReg package. This approach essentially compresses the data and removes zeros, allowing the use of models that rely on log-ratios.

Mixture CoDa Models:
Alternatively, you could explore mixture models for CoDa, as described in Section 5 of the following paper: Figueira et al., 2024 – Handling zeros in compositional data using Bayesian mixture models <https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21695>.
This approach provides a more flexible framework for dealing with zeros without the need for transformations that remove them.

Best!

Joaquín

Could somebody please help me setting a latent effect of size 2n?

Thank you very much. I attach an application example
Best,
LC

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Double hurdle model
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

This model can in principle be written as a nonlinear inlabru model,
via predictors
  eta_encounter = qlogis(1-(1-plogis(eta_c1))*(1-plogis(eta_c2)))
  eta_positive = log(exp(c1)+exp(c2))

However, as written, there is no way to identify the relative
contributions from "small" and "large", making the model
nonidentifiable.
Do you have any observations that distinguish between "small" and
"large"? Without that, I don't think one can get useful inference from
it, partly due to multimodality, but also the fundamental
nonidentifiability.

Treating a total count as y ~ Poisson(exp(c1)+exp(c2)) is appropriate
if the "small" count is y1 ~ Poisson(exp(c1)) and the "large" count is
y2 ~ Poisson(exp(c2)), since the sum of two (independent) Poisson
variables is Poisson.
The hurdle model then needs a truncated poisson model, "nzpoisson",
not a full Poisson model.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Double hurdle model
messages.body_plain:
The idea in the hurdle model construction is that the positive counts
are modelled conditionally on there being at least one, and to not
scale the parameter by 1/(1-(1-p1)*(1-p2)).
But I see the point about whether the combined model actually has a
nzpoisson structure at all.

If y1 and y2 are the small and large counts (from 0 and upwards), we have
p_y1(x) ~ I(x=0) (1-p1) + p1 * I(x>0) p_nzp(x;c1) (i.e. a hurdle model
with 0/1 and nzpoisson)
p_y2(x) ~ I(x=0) (1-p2) + p2 * I(x>0) p_nzp(x;c2)

The question is then what distribution the sum y = y1+y2 has, and
whether that can be written on the same hurdle form.

For the sum of two independent random variables, we get
  p_y(z) = \sum_{x=0}^z p_y1(x) p_y2(z-x)

I suspect this doesn't result in an expression of the form
  I(z=0) (1-py) + py * I(z>0) p_nzp(z;cy)
which would be required for the model to be the true combined result
of the building blocks y1 and y2.

But a good approximation might be had by working out what the expected
value of y is, and then choosing a regular hurdle model where the
parameter is chosen to give that overall expectation.

E(y1+y2) = p1 * c1 / (1 - exp(-c1)) + p2 * c2 / (1 - exp(-c2))
  and
E(y) = py * cy / (1-exp(-cy))

and since the nonzero probability is known to be py = 1-(1-p1)*(1-p2),
that gives a nonlinear equation to solve for cy to make the
expectations equal, and log(cy) could then be used as the predictor
expression in a regular hurdle model.
How good this approximation might be I don't know (and it's possible
that your suggestion is close to this as well).
I'm also not sure how practical this would be to implement and use!

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am working on modeling extreme events using the Generalized Pareto (GP) distribution in INLA. My dataset consists of multiple stations, each with multiple observations over time. Each observation​ ys,t represents the exceedance for station s at time point t. At this stage, I am not including any covariates in the model.

After fitting the model, I plan to compute return levels using the quantile of the GP distribution at a specified cumulative probability:
x_p=F^(-1) (ρ,σ,ξ)
 where p=1-  1/(T )

and T is the return period.
I assume a constant shape parameter ξ across all stations.
However, I need different return levels per station.
The scale parameter σ in the INLA formulation depends on the linear predictor and is estimated at the level of each individual observation rather than per station.

Is there a way in INLA to obtain return levels at the station level, rather than for each individual observation? Ideally, I would like a single return level per station for each return period.

Any guidance on how to structure this in a hierarchical setting within INLA would be greatly appreciated!
